| Account | What the provider reports | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek | The prepaid API **balance**, in yuan or dollars, and the part of it that was granted | A limit, or what you spent |
| OpenRouter | What is **left of the key's spending limit** in dollars, or what the key has used when it has no limit; and its spend today and this month | Your account's credit balance, which needs a management key Milo does not ask for |
| Devin | **ACUs** your organization consumed in Devin's current billing day, which starts at 08:00 UTC | What is left of a plan. Enterprise plans only |
| Copilot | GitHub **AI credits** your personal account consumed this calendar month | What is left of the monthly allowance, which the API does not report. Not for seats billed to an organization |

These are money and counts, so they are written out in words, such as `DeepSeek · ¥110.00 balance` or `Devin · 12.5 ACUs today`. They are never drawn as a percentage or a large figure, never pick the menu bar badge and never raise a low-quota alert. An answer older than two refreshes is marked with its age; one older than a day, or from a billing day or month that has ended, is dropped.

**Turn an account on** under **Usage** in `milo web`, or in `~/.config/milo/preferences.conf` (a worktree can have its own choice, like the tools):

```
usage_deepseek = auto
usage_openrouter = always
usage_devin = hide
usage_copilot = hide
```

**Auto** asks the provider and gives the account a place once it has a figure. **Always show** also keeps the place to say why there is none, such as `no key set`, `key was refused` or `rate limited`. Terminal Settings (`milo setup`) does not list accounts yet.

**Give Milo a key of its own.** Milo reads only these names, from the environment of the shell that starts the pane, or from `~/.config/milo/usage-accounts.conf`:

| Account | Settings | The key |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DeepSeek | `MILO_DEEPSEEK_API_KEY` | An API key from the DeepSeek platform |
| OpenRouter | `MILO_OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | An ordinary API key; one with its own spending limit shows what is left of it |
| Devin | `MILO_DEVIN_API_KEY`, `MILO_DEVIN_ORG` (`org-…`) | A service user key or personal access token with the `ViewOrgConsumption` permission |
| Copilot | `MILO_GITHUB_TOKEN`, `MILO_GITHUB_USER` | A fine-grained personal access token with read access to the account's **Plan** |

```
# ~/.config/milo/usage-accounts.conf — chmod 600
MILO_DEEPSEEK_API_KEY = sk-…
```

The file must be a plain file of yours that no one else can read, or Milo ignores it and says so. The environment wins over the file. The macOS menu bar app does not inherit your shell's environment, so it needs the file. Milo does not look at `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY`, `GH_TOKEN` or any key another tool keeps: a key reaches a provider only because you named it for Milo. Prefer a key made for this, with the least access the provider offers. A DeepSeek key can also spend the balance, so treat the file like the key itself.

**What is sent and kept.** One `GET` over HTTPS to the provider's own host, through `/usr/bin/curl`, with the key passed on curl's standard input rather than its command line. Redirects are not followed. DeepSeek and OpenRouter are asked at most every 5 minutes, Devin and Copilot every 15, and once more when the billing day or month their count covers ends. `r` asks again, but no sooner than 30 seconds after the last request and never inside a rate limit the provider announced. A refused key is not offered again for 30 minutes unless you press `r`. The figures and times of the last answer are saved under `~/.local/state/milo/accounts/` so that every pane and the menu share one request; the key is never written there.

**Where it appears.** Limits keep their rows first, then OpenCode, then accounts: one row each at the foot of the pane, or the whole pane when no tool has a place. The menu lists each account with its figure in words.

Using DeepSeek or OpenRouter through OpenCode shows two different things: OpenCode's estimate of what today's steps cost, and what the provider says is left. Milo shows each under its own name and does not combine them.

## What milo does not do

For the tools above, the usage pane reads local data. It does not call their providers, run the tools, sign in, read their saved credentials, guess limits from token counts or work out a cost from them. Figures can be old or missing if no tool has saved a report on this machine recently. The status-line helper writes its own limit readings, not the session logs.

The one exception is an [account you turn on](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage.md#accounts-asked-online). For that account alone Milo sends one request to the provider's documented endpoint, with a key you set for Milo. It never turns a balance, a spend or a count of credits into a percentage, never adds figures from different accounts together, and never uses a key another tool saved.

## If a figure is missing

- A tool that is not there at all has no figure saved on this Mac, or is hidden. Run `milo doctor` to see what Milo found, or choose **Always show** for it in setup to keep its place and see what it is waiting for.
- Make the pane taller and wider to see labels, reset times and hints. Where the terminal can show pictures, including in Rex, milo draws the logos and large figures as pictures. Otherwise it draws with text. Short panes use text either way.
- Press `r` to check local data immediately. Milo reuses any oh-my-pi check already in progress and updates the pane when it finishes. Existing figures stay visible; `checking` means a lookup is in progress and there is no figure yet. For a tool, reload does not ask a provider for a fresh reading; for an account you turned on, it asks again at most every 30 seconds.
- A tool that is always shown, or found while no tool has a figure, says why it has none. `no sessions found` means no Codex sessions were found; `no limits to show` means there are sessions but no usable limits, or that a saved report has no windows. `no saved limits found` means milo has no saved Claude Code reading. `no tokens recorded today` means OpenCode's database has nothing from today. A narrow pane may shorten these hints.
- For oh-my-pi, check that `/usr/bin/sqlite3` is available and the harness has saved a report. For Claude Code, see [setup](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/setup.md#claude-code-limits) if neither saved source has a reading.
- An account that is turned on but missing has no figure yet and is set to Auto. Run `milo doctor`: it names the setting each account reads, where it found the key, and what the last answer or failure was, without asking the provider again. Choose **Always show** to see the reason in the pane. On a two-row rail with two limits, raise **Usage height** to give an account a row.

---

Source: https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md

# Discord presence

Milo can show on your Discord profile that you are using Rex. It is off until you turn it on, and while it is off Milo starts nothing for it and never contacts Discord.

## What becomes public

While presence is on and a Rex app has a session open on this computer, the Discord app shows this as your activity:

- **Milo's name and icon**, from Milo's public Discord application
- one fixed line under it: **In a Rex session**

Anyone who can see your Discord activity sees it, and so can tell when you are using Rex. Discord decides who that is and may add how long the activity has been up. Use Discord's own activity privacy settings to narrow it.

That is all, unless you choose to show more. There are four choices of **details**, and the first is the default:

| Details | Adds a second line | For example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `generic` | nothing | |
| `session` | the name of the Rex session in front | Session: release-notes |
| `project` | the folder name of the Git project in that session's focused pane | Project: milo |
| `both` | both names | Project: milo · Session: release-notes |

A session's name is whatever you or a coding agent called it, and often describes the work, so read it as others would before showing it. A project's name is the folder name of its Git repository: never its path, its remote address or a branch.

Whatever you choose, Milo never sends a tab title, a file name, a path, a remote address, a command, a terminal title or anything a terminal shows. Each name is cut to one short line of plain text. A name that could be a path or an address, one with a `/`, a `\` or a `user@host:` form, is left out whole.

Every place you can turn presence on, or choose to show a name, says what that makes public before it does. Turning presence on does not turn names on, and a choice saved by an earlier Milo keeps showing only what it showed then.

### Which session is “in front”

Names come only from the session the Rex app on this computer is showing: the one whose active tab has its focused pane held by that app. Rex has no call that names the session an app is looking at, so Milo goes by that. If two sessions fit, or none does, Milo shows no name at all rather than the name of the wrong session, and `milo presence` says so. This happens once the app has shown more than one session, or while only a phone or another computer is attached. Outside a Git project there is no project name.

With `generic`, Milo asks Rex one thing: whether any Rex app has a session open. It looks at no session. With a name chosen, it also asks which session is in front and, only for the names you chose, that session's label and the folder its focused pane is working in.

## Turn it on

Nothing needs creating first: Milo shows the activity under its own Discord application. An application ID is public, not a password. Milo holds no bot, token or client secret, and never signs in to Discord.

Use any one of these:

- `milo presence enable`. It says what becomes public and asks before turning anything on. `--yes` answers for you in a script.
- `milo setup`, then **Workflow → Discord presence**.
- `milo web`, then **Integrations → Discord presence → Turn on…**.

All three read and write the same saved choice, `discord.conf` in Milo's settings folder. It is one choice for your account on this computer, not a per-worktree preference, and it is saved at once without the **Save** step that pane preferences use.

To show a name, choose it in the same place: `milo presence details session`, `project`, `both` or back to `generic`; **Presence shows** in Settings; or **Shows** in the browser editor. While presence is on, a choice that adds a name asks first, and one that removes a name takes it down at once.

### Your own application

To show a name and icon of your choosing in place of Milo's:

1. Open <https://discord.com/developers/applications>, choose **New Application** and name it. The name is what Discord shows, as in “Playing Rex”. An app icon is optional. No bot is needed.
2. Copy the **Application ID** from its General Information page. It is a number of 17 to 19 digits.
3. Give it to Milo: `milo presence application APPLICATION_ID`, **Presence application** in Settings, or **Use your own Discord app** in the browser editor. A terminal's paste is not read in Settings, so the command is easier for a copied ID.

`milo presence application official`, or the same control in Settings and the browser editor, goes back to Milo's. An application ID you saved with an earlier Milo is kept until you do.

## Check it and turn it off

`milo presence` says whether presence is on, which application and details it uses, and what Discord is showing now, names included. The same line appears under **Discord presence** in Settings, in the browser editor and in `milo doctor`.

| It says | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Discord is showing “In a Rex session”. | The activity is up, with any names it lists. |
| …with no name: Milo has none it can be sure of. | Names are chosen, but [no one session is in front](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md#which-session-is-in-front) or it has no name to show. |
| Nothing is shown until a Rex app opens a session. | Rex is running, but no Rex app has a session open. |
| The Discord app is not running here. | Milo looks for it every 10 seconds while Rex is in use. |
| Discord does not know this application ID. | Check the ID, or go back to Milo's application. |
| Milo's presence helper is not running. | See [when it runs](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md#when-it-runs). |
| Discord did not accept the activity. | Discord answered with an error. Nothing is shown until presence is turned on again or Rex restarts. |

`milo presence disable`, or the same switch in Settings or the browser editor, takes the activity down at once, closes Milo's connection to Discord and stops the helper. Nothing then runs until you turn presence on again. Your choice of details and application is kept.

## When it runs

While presence is on, one small helper process does the work. Rex tells it when the first Rex app opens a session and when the last one leaves; it puts the activity up and takes it down to match. However many tabs, sessions and Milo panes are open, there is one helper and one connection to Discord, so nothing competes to set your activity.

With names chosen, Rex also tells the helper when a tab, a pane, a session's name or a pane's program changes. The helper waits a second for such changes to settle, and tells Discord only if the line it would show is different. Changing the details or the application replaces the helper: the old activity is taken down before the new one is put up.

The helper starts when you turn presence on while Rex is running, and whenever Rex loads Milo's saved layout, which is each time Rex starts once you have saved a layout in `milo setup` with at least one pane or with **Arrange new shell tabs** on. It ends when the Rex server stops. Without a saved layout, run `milo presence enable` again after starting Rex.

If Discord is not running, or quits, the helper waits and puts the activity back within about 10 seconds of Discord returning. Quitting Rex or turning presence off takes the activity down. So does **Uninstall Milo** in Home, which also turns presence off, so a later install starts with it off. If you remove the binary another way, run `milo presence disable` first. Rex itself is never slowed or changed by any of this: the helper only listens.

## Platforms and limits

- Presence talks to the **Discord desktop app** on the same computer and account as Milo, through the [local connection Discord documents](https://docs.discord.com/developers/topics/rpc). The browser and mobile versions of Discord have none, and nothing is shown through them alone.
- Milo's prebuilt release is for Apple Silicon Macs. A source build on Linux looks for Discord's socket in `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` as Discord documents; a Discord installed as a Flatpak or Snap keeps its socket elsewhere and is not found.
- Only a Rex app with a session open counts. Scripts, the `rex` command and Milo's own listener do not, and a Rex app left open counts for as long as it has a session open, whether or not you are at the keyboard.
- Presence follows the Rex server on this computer. Sessions on another host do not start it there, and names are never taken from them.
- Names are shown only [when one session is plainly in front](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md#which-session-is-in-front). Expect the fixed line alone after you have looked at several sessions.
- The fixed line's wording cannot be changed. To change the name or icon, use [an application of your own](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md#your-own-application).
- If Discord rejects an application ID, Milo stops asking until you turn presence on again or Rex restarts.

---

Source: https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/skills/milo/SKILL.md

---
name: milo
description: Use milo in a user's terminal to show a Git file tree, recent commits, usage, or a file from the working tree or a commit, and to guide Rex setup.
---

# milo

## Check first

- Run `command -v milo` and `milo --version` in the environment where the pane
  will run. A version confirms the binary is available, not that Rex is set up.
- In this checkout, `milo doctor` explains effective preferences, integration
  health and usage sources without changing anything. For an older installed
  binary, check `milo --help`; `rex actions` (without `-C` or `REX_CLIENT`)
  lists server actions such as `milo_layout`.
- Open `milo setup` for interactive configuration. Trying a layout is not
  permission to save it. Distinguish the global default from the override for
  this Git worktree. `milo_remember_layout` captures an explicitly chosen rail;
  `milo_peek_outline` opens a temporary floating outline instead of docking it.
- With **Title Rex tabs** on, Milo names tabs nobody has named for their Git
  project, worktree and agent. A tab you or the user rename keeps that name and
  Milo stops titling it. Milo never renames a session on its own.
  `milo_name_session` renames the session it is run in after the project of
  the given shell. It creates and switches to nothing. Run it only when the
  user asks for that name.
- Use `milo setup --repair` or `--remove` only when asked to change the
  integration. Do not change Rex's global theme, font or keyboard shortcuts.
- Discord presence is off unless the user turned it on, and it publishes on
  their Discord profile. `milo presence` reports it without changing anything.
  Run `milo presence enable`, `details`, `application` or `disable` only when
  the user asks, and never pass `--yes` for them: it skips the notice of what
  becomes public. Never raise the details to `session`, `project` or `both`
  on your own: they show the session's name or the project's folder name.

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `milo` | Opens the interactive home menu. |
| `milo setup --skip-onboarding` | Dismisses the first-run guide and exits without a TUI or installation changes. |
| `milo outline [PATH]` | Shows a live file tree with changes to commit or push. |
| `milo history [PATH]` | Shows recent commits and the files they touched. |
| `milo usage` | Shows local usage limits and today's activity for whichever of Codex, Claude Code and OpenCode have saved a figure. |
| `milo view FILE [--commit ID \| --edit]` | Opens the reader. It only reads unless the user presses `e` or you pass `--edit`, which starts editing a working text file. |
| `milo setup` | Chooses a Rex layout and optionally enables Claude Code limits. |
| `milo web [--port PORT] [--no-open]` | Opens the settings dashboard on loopback. Check `milo web --help` for availability on older installs. |
| `milo presence [status]` | Says whether the optional Discord presence is on and what Discord shows now. |
| `milo listen [--stop]` | Starts or stops layout memory, automatic new-tab arrangement and tab titles; normally managed by setup. |
| `milo claude-status` | Status-line helper called by Claude Code, not a pane. |

`PATH` defaults to the current directory. Use direct pane commands when launching a pane for the user; they bypass the home menu and onboarding. Use `milo --help` for the CLI guide and `?` for pane keys.

## Open a file for the user

In an interactive terminal, use `milo view "$file"` for the working copy or
`milo view "$file" --commit "$id"` for the file as of a commit. For the second
form, start at the repository root, use the path relative to that root as it
existed at the commit, and pass a full or abbreviated hex Git commit ID.

To open a reader from a non-interactive agent shell, start a terminal tab in
the user's intended Rex session. Pass the file and commit as separate quoted
arguments. For example, with the session and project directory identified:

```sh
rex run -s "$session" -c "$project_dir" -- milo view "$file"
rex run -s "$session" -c "$project_dir" -- milo view "$file" --commit "$id"
```

The user can press `n` or `N` to move between changed blocks and `q` or `Esc`
to close the reader. In Rex, opening a file from the outline or history also
opens a floating reader.

The reader does not change a file unless the user edits and saves it. `e`
starts an edit of a working text file, `Ctrl-S` saves, `Ctrl-F` formats the
draft with a formatter already installed, and `Esc` stops, asking first if
there are unsaved changes. Use `milo view "$file" --edit` only when the user
asked to edit that file. Do not type into the user's editor or answer its
questions for them; to change a file yourself, use your own tools.

## Do not

- Do not edit the user's Rex or Claude Code configuration directly. Use
  `milo setup` and save only with the user's approval.
- Do not paste the private URL printed by `milo web` into chats, logs or issues:
  it includes the session key. For local use, let Milo open the browser.
- Do not run full-screen panes in your own non-interactive shell. They need
  an interactive terminal. If you cannot target the user's terminal, give
  the user the command to run instead.

---

Source: https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md

# Contributing to milo

Keep changes small and make milo simpler, faster or more correct.

## Getting set up

You need Rust 1.91 or later, git, and a terminal.

CI checks every target and runs the portable test suite on Linux with Rust 1.91.0 and SQLite installed. Keep the Apple Silicon job too: filesystem notifications, terminal images and the packaged browser editor have platform-specific behavior.

Set `fork_url` to the URL of a fork you can access, then run:

```sh
git clone "$fork_url" milo
cd milo
cargo build --release
./target/release/milo outline    # the outline, in this repository
./target/release/milo history    # recent commits
./target/release/milo usage      # usage at a glance
./target/release/milo view src/main.rs
```

## Before you open a pull request

Run these checks:

```sh
cargo build --release              # no warnings
cargo clippy --all-targets         # no warnings; the lint set is in Cargo.toml
cargo fmt -- --check               # no diff; the settings are in rustfmt.toml
cargo test                         # everything passes
```

After changing `install.sh`, also run `sh tests/install.sh`; `cargo test` does not run it.

Then run the program and look at what you changed. Text checks cannot tell you whether a pane looks right.

When updating the README, guides, agent skill, `llms.txt` or this file, run `python3 site/bundle-docs.py` and commit the refreshed `site/public/llms-full.txt` and `site/public/llms.txt`. CI checks that the published copies match these sources.

The website in `site/` is a Next.js static export, built with Bun 1.4 and Node.js 26. In that directory, `bun install` and `bun run dev` start it for editing. Before a pull request, run `bun test && bun run build`, then `bun run preview` and look at the built pages in a browser. Railway runs the same build and serves `site/dist` with `site/Caddyfile`.

Describe the pull request under the headings in `.github/pull_request_template.md`: **What changed** and **Verification**. GitHub fills them in when you open a pull request in the browser. A body passed on the command line (`gh pr create --body` or `--body-file`) replaces the template, so write the same headings yourself. Add **Compatibility** when a user or packager has to act.

A pull request that changes anything you can see (the website, a terminal pane, the macOS app or any other visible surface) must show real screenshots of the affected UI under **Screenshots** in its description. Show before and after when it changes an existing design, and desktop and mobile when both are affected. A change with nothing to see needs no screenshot; leave the section out.

Give every screenshot alt text that says what it shows, for people who cannot see the image: `![Changes pane after the fix, with the deleted file listed once](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/…)`. GitHub's default, the file name, says nothing. Replace it, in `alt="…"` too when GitHub inserts an `<img>` tag.

Label the pull request with the existing labels that fit, not every one that could. Usually that is one kind and one or two areas:

- **Kind:** `bug`, `enhancement` or `documentation`.
- **Area:** `ux` for what the user sees or does, `integrations` for Rex, coding agents and usage sources, `reliability` for recovery and regression checks, `performance` for speed and resource use, `accessibility` for barriers to people with disabilities.
- **State:** `in review` once it is ready to be read.

Nothing adds these for you, except that Dependabot labels its own pull requests. If GitHub does not let you set labels, say which fit and a maintainer will add them. Do not create new labels in a pull request.

## Tagging a release

Push the release commit to `main`, then wait for **Apple Silicon release tests** to pass on that exact commit before creating its tag. On an arm64 macOS runner, GitHub Actions runs `sh tests/install.sh` and `cargo test --release --locked`, then drives the browser editor of a release build in Chromium with `tests/web-smoke.cjs`. GitHub requires that check for tag creation and updates, including when a release creates its tag through the web UI. If releasing from another branch, run **Release tests** on that branch from the Actions tab first.

## What a good change looks like

**It solves one thing.** A bug fix does not also rename a module. A refactoring does not also change behaviour.

**It adds no dependency.** milo depends on `libc` and nothing else. If you believe a crate would earn its place, open an issue first and say what it replaces.

**It is tested by what the user sees.** Use throwaway Git repositories (`src/fixture.rs`) and check the frames the program draws where practical. Write tests that would fail if the behaviour broke, not tests that repeat the code. A bug fix comes with the test that would have caught it.

**It keeps untrusted repositories safe.** Keep the user's Git settings, but disable hooks, filters, external diffs, text converters, file-system monitors and on-demand fetching. Do not follow a folder link out of the project to show a file or let names and messages send terminal controls.

**It keeps subprocesses in one place per tool.** Start Git through `src/git/run.rs`, `/usr/bin/sips` through `src/picture.rs`, `/usr/bin/sqlite3` through `src/usage/sqlite.rs`, `/usr/bin/curl` through `src/usage/http.rs` or `src/alerts/send.rs`, `/usr/bin/security` through `src/alerts/secret.rs`, Rex through `src/rex.rs`, and formatters through `src/format.rs`. Use their existing safeguards. Never run a command named by project files or Git settings.

**It writes to a project only when the user saves.** Every git command milo runs only reads. The one thing that changes a project is `Ctrl-S` in the reader's editor, and it goes through `src/reader/disk.rs`: the file is opened without following a link, read again, and written only if it is still what the edit started from or the user says to overwrite it. Do not add a second way to write, and do not let anything else (a formatter, a cache, a temporary file) write into the project. What milo keeps for itself, such as a draft from a reader that was ended, goes in its state folder.

**It starts no program the user did not ask for.** Opening and showing a file never run anything from the project or for it. A formatter runs only on `Ctrl-F`, is found by a fixed name in the folders of `PATH` written in full, and is given the draft on standard input. Never install, download or run a tool through a package runner.

## Style

The code is written to be read. A few habits keep it that way:

- **Comments say what and why, in plain words.** Write for someone who knows Rust but has never seen this file. Do not describe how the code used to be, and do not restate the line below.
- **One word per idea.** *Pending* is anything not yet pushed; *uncommitted* is the part of that not yet committed; *unpushed* is the part committed but still local. `check` takes in changes made outside; `poll` asks git whether anything moved; `load` rebuilds what a screen shows. If you need a new word, define it in a doc comment where the idea is introduced.
- **Small functions with one job.** If a function runs past about forty lines and is not a plain table, it is probably doing two things.
- **Names over positions.** Prefer a small struct or enum to a tuple or a bare `bool` argument when a reader would otherwise have to remember an order or a meaning.
- **No leftovers.** No commented-out code, no `TODO`, no parameter that is always the same value, no helper kept for a caller that is gone.
- **`unsafe` explains itself.** Every block has a `// SAFETY:` comment directly above it giving the actual argument. The lints enforce that the comment exists; reviewers check that it is true.
- **On screen, plain words.** Text the user reads says "changed", "to commit", "to push". Words such as *pending* are for the code.

## Finding your way around

The [source map](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#source-map) lists the files under `src/` and `tests/`.

### Adding a pane

Put the pane in a module under `src/` and implement `pane::Pane`: `draw` fills a `Screen`, `help` returns its own `Page::new` guide, and `key` handles pane-specific input. Return `After::Leave` to close, `After::Stay` to draw again, or `After::Ignored` to keep the frame. For outside changes, add `watch_scope` and `check`; for timed redraws, add `next_frame`. A pane with no watch or timer sleeps until input, resize or a signal.

Declare the module in `src/main.rs`. Add the command to `Command`, the argument parser, `dispatch` and `--help`. Use the shared loop; choose whether the pane starts loaded, does a first check or shows `Reading…` on a slow open.

### Changing the Rex layout

The two Lua templates are in `src/setup/`. `layout.rs` adds the choices and
proportions above the actions in `rex.lua`, and the path to that file above
the handler in `listener.lua`. `rex_files.rs` asks Rex to check changed
generated files before writing settings. The listener snapshots existing rails
after Rex attaches, without replacing a baseline already captured from an event.

`setup/profiles.rs` stores rail geometry separately from those integration files.
Persist roles, side, order and proportions, never Rex block IDs. A trial is the
exception: its IDs are transient and are the only blocks its undo may close.
`preferences.rs` resolves pane settings outside the repository, per worktree
over global defaults. `workflow.rs` and `rex_shell.lua` follow only the shell
explicitly supplied by a managed pane. Ordinary manual pane launches stay pinned.

An installation keeps the Lua files it was saved with until its next save, and
a save replaces only files it recognises as Milo's. Before changing
`actions.lua` or `listener.lua`, add the fingerprint (`fingerprint` in
`layout.rs`, the 64-bit FNV-1a of the file) of the version being replaced to
the list beside it, or installations holding that version are told their file
was left alone. `listener_0_1_2.lua` is the listener of releases 0.1.1 and
0.1.2, kept so that a test can save over it.

`titles.rs` names tabs and sessions for the listener and the session action,
and keeps the titles Milo set by Rex window ID in the state folder. A title
may use folder names and an agent's process name. Never read a terminal's
title, screen or status text for it, and never replace a label that is neither
Rex's default nor Milo's own. Only `milo_name_session` names a session, and
only the one it is run in: never rename, create or switch a session from the
listener or as a side effect of another action.

The listener keeps the answers of `milo tab-title title` by directory, so that
most events start no process. Each answer lists its grounds, the files that
decide it, and is reused while they read the same: a project's two preference
files, or outside a project the places where a repository could appear. When
neither says enough, as when Git could not run, list none and the listener
asks again. The listener opens every file listed, so never list a path that
another user could create.

Run `cargo test setup::` for generation, screen and installation tests. The
tests use throwaway settings and a stand-in for Rex. With Lua 5.1 installed,
run `cargo test --locked --bin milo rex_lua_fixtures -- --ignored` for the
action and listener scenarios. Set `LUA51` if the executable is not `lua5.1`.
No running Rex session is needed. To check a generated
file with Rex itself, run `MILO_CHECKING_REX=1 rex config check /path/to/copy.lua`
on a scratch copy. The flag prevents the actions file starting a listener
during the check. Check both files and try the pane choices. Only try a
reload or the actions on a disposable Rex configuration and session, never
as part of `cargo test`.

With Rex installed, `cargo test --test rex_lab -- --ignored --nocapture` does
that for you. It starts a Rex server of its own in a throwaway folder, with its
own home, settings, state and socket. There it saves a layout and follows two
Git worktrees through new tabs, divider drags, renamed tabs and sessions, and a
restart of the server. Every `rex` the test runs names that socket and cannot
start another server, and it checks that the lab's terminals and listener use
the lab's home and server too, so the Rex you are working in is never asked
anything. On macOS a shell tab runs under `login`, which hands it your home
again, so the lab sets `ZDOTDIR` and checks that each shell read the lab's
startup file and not yours. That file makes the shell copy itself a few times
as it starts, which is what prompts and plugins do to a shell while its new
tab is being arranged. Set `MILO_TEST_REX` if `rex` is not on your path. The test prints
whether the restarted server ran Milo again in the panes it restored; that is
Rex's choice. Where it restored shells instead, the test rebuilds one such rail
with the two actions `docs/setup.md` gives for that, and sees its drags
remembered again. A new shell tab that does not get its rail fails the test: none
is opened in its place. That holds for the tabs the test opens one at a time
and for those it opens back to back, four with no pause between them, three
times over.

A second test there, on a server of its own, is for the floating reader. It
opens a file from the outline, edits and saves it through keys Rex sends, sees
the outline leave that reader alone while it has unsaved changes, then has Rex
close the reader on an unsaved draft and gets the draft back at the next edit.

### Changing alert mirroring

`src/alerts.rs` and the files under `src/alerts/` mirror Rex alerts to Telegram or Discord. An *alert* is an event Rex itself draws attention to; `event.rs` lists them and is the only place that decides. Hear Rex only through `rex events`, as `src/rex.rs` starts it: never read a terminal's screen, a system notification or Rex's socket for an alert.

Mirroring stays off until the user turns it on. The setup screen and the browser editor say what will be sent and ask first; `milo alerts` says it before and `milo alerts on` as it starts. A new field leaves the machine only behind a choice that is off by default, and `message.rs` says so in `sends`. Whatever a program supplied, its short name included, is untrusted: send it through `literal`, and its text through `plain` first.

A secret goes from standard input or the browser editor to `secret.rs` and from there to curl's standard input. Never put one in an argument, a settings file, a status note, a log, or anything sent back to a settings page. Destinations are fixed hosts; do not add one the user can type.

`cargo test alerts` runs the unit tests and `cargo test --test alerts` runs the real `milo alerts` against stand-ins: a `rex` that prints the events a test writes, and a server on the loopback address for both destinations. `MILO_ALERTS_TEST_ENDPOINT` names that server, and is refused unless it is `http://127.0.0.1:PORT`. On macOS `MILO_ALERTS_KEYCHAIN` names a keychain file of the test's own, so that tests never touch yours. Only a development build reads either variable: a release build has no setting that changes where a secret is kept or sent, so with `--release` these tests do nothing. No test may use a real token, webhook or chat, or post to Telegram or Discord.

To try it against Rex itself, use a disposable server as `tests/rex_lab.rs` does and a development build, with those two variables set and a local server in place of the destinations. A program in a lab terminal raises a synthetic alert with `printf '\033]7501;state=blocked:kind=permission:app=synthetic\033\\'`.

### Changing Discord presence

[Discord presence](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/presence.md) publishes an activity to Discord. It stays off until someone turns it on, and off means no process, no socket and no timer: `tests/presence.rs` checks that. The activity is the fixed line in `src/presence/discord.rs`, under Milo's public application ID or one the person gave. Milo holds no bot, token or secret for either, and none may be added.

A second line is shown only for the *details* a person chose: the name of the session in front, the folder name of the Git project in its focused pane, or both. The default shows neither, and a choice saved by an earlier release must go on showing only what it showed. `src/rex_presence.lua` may look at sessions only for a name that was chosen, and never reads a tab's or terminal's title, a screen, a command line or a status text. Every name goes through `src/presence/label.rs`, which keeps one short line of plain text and drops whole anything that could be a path or an address. Never show a path, a remote address, a branch, a file name or a command, by default or behind a setting. When the script cannot tell which one session is in front, it reports none, and no name is shown. `presence::public` says what each choice shows, and every surface shows that text before turning presence on or adding a name.

`presence::Control` is the only way to read or change the choice, so `milo presence`, Settings and the browser editor cannot disagree. One helper holds `presence.lock` for as long as it runs; a second gives up rather than set the activity in turn. A change to the details or the application replaces the helper, which takes the old activity down first.

No test may reach a real Discord. The helper looks for Discord's socket in one folder, the first of `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `TMPDIR`, `TMP` and `TEMP` that is set, so a test that starts a helper gives it an environment in which the first of those names a folder of the test's own, and listens there as a stand-in. Do the same when trying a build by hand, and do not publish to your own Discord account from a test. With Rex installed, `cargo test --test rex_lab -- --ignored discord_presence` checks the watch on a disposable Rex server. What a real Discord app then displays can only be checked by hand with a test application and account.

### Adding a usage source

[Usage sources](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/usage-sources.md) has the rules a source must meet and the evidence for each harness looked at so far. Before writing a reader, check the tool's format against a pinned release: in its source, and in a file that release wrote under a throwaway home. Keep tokens, cost and limits as separate values, and leave unknown whatever the tool does not save. Copy the structure of test fixtures from the release, and record the release and its checksum beside them. Read databases through `src/usage/sqlite.rs` and session files through `src/usage/files.rs` so every read stays bounded.

A tool also needs a rule for when it is found on this machine, apart from whether it has a figure, and an entry in `UsageTool` in `src/preferences.rs` so that it can be always shown or hidden. Decide it from files the tool saved, never by running the tool. A tool that is absent or hidden must take no room in the pane, in its help or in `milo doctor`, and a hidden one must not be looked for. `src/usage/tests/tools.rs` checks this at every size class.

An account is different: its figure exists only on a provider's servers, so nothing on disk says it is in use. It needs an entry in `UsageAccount`, which starts hidden, and an adapter in `src/usage/accounts.rs` that names the documented endpoint, the `MILO_…` settings it reads, how often it may be asked, and how to read the reply into a `Figure` with its own `Kind` and `Unit`. Never give an account a limit window: a balance, a spend or a count of credits must not become a percentage or reach the menu bar badge. Never read a key another tool saved, and never test against the real provider. Unit tests serve fixtures from a loopback port through `Sources::test`. That stand-in and the plain-HTTP address it uses are compiled only under `cfg(test)`: an installed binary has no setting, variable or file that sends a key anywhere but the provider's HTTPS host, and `tests/pane.rs` checks the built binary for that. Do not add one.

### Adding a language to the reader

Code colouring uses `src/syntax.rs` for scanning, `src/syntax/langs.rs` for language tables, and `src/syntax/delimiters.rs` for strings and comments whose closing marks depend on the opener. `src/syntax/markup.rs` reads HTML and XML, and `src/syntax/markdown.rs` reads Markdown; those two are not code and have walkers of their own. Adding a language normally means changing only the tables:

1. Add a `Lang` constant: its line and block comments, its quotes (list a longer opener before any opener it starts with), its keywords and constants.
2. Map its file extensions in `FILE_LANGS`, or a file name such as `Makefile` in `NAMED_LANGS`.
3. Add a test with a few idiomatic lines and the classes you expect.
4. Add its row to the language table in `docs/panes.md`.

The scanner is not a parser and is not meant to become one. It knows comments, strings, numbers and reserved words, and guesses types and calls from how a name is written. If a language needs more than a table can say, it is fine for milo to colour it imperfectly. A search for a closer must not start again from every opener on a line: a line can be megabytes long.

### Adding a formatter

`src/format.rs` has the table of formatters: `KINDS` maps file extensions to the tools tried in order, and each `Tool` is a program's name and its arguments. A formatter belongs there only if it reads the text on standard input and writes the formatted text to standard output, leaves the file alone, needs no network and exits with a failure when it cannot format. Give it the file's name with `Name`, which is passed as `./name` so that it cannot be read as an option.

1. Check the command against the real program, including what it does with text it cannot parse and whether it writes a cache into the folder it runs in.
2. Add the `Tool` and its row in `KINDS`, with the names as they read in `Not installed: …`. Keep those names within 24 characters: they are a row of the help page.
3. Add the row to the formatter table in `docs/panes.md`.

The tests use stand-ins written by `format::tests::stand_in`, so they pass on a machine with no formatter installed. `rustfmt_formats_a_rust_draft_where_it_is_installed` in `tests/pane.rs` runs the real program where there is one.

### Checking failures and speed

`src/usage/tests/failures.rs` breaks each local usage source in five ways: missing, rotated, locked, stale, and written in a shape Milo does not know. The pane may then show only a figure the source reported, marked as old once it is; a source that cannot be read is unknown. A new source goes through the same five tests with its own files, using the helpers there.

`src/usage/tests/accounts.rs` does the same for accounts against a loopback server: a missing key, a settings file others can read, a refused key, a rate limit, an unreachable provider, an old answer and a reply in an unknown shape.

`tests/reader_bench.rs` times the reader of a release build on generated files: long lines, comments and strings that span lines, and diffs just under the size Milo loads. It measures the first frame that shows the file and the frame after each key, through a real terminal:

```sh
cargo test --release --locked --test reader_bench -- --ignored --nocapture
sh tests/reader-compare.sh REVISION > report.tsv    # this checkout beside that revision
```

`tests/reader-compare.sh` exports the revision, builds it in a temporary folder and times both builds turn about, so the two columns come from the same machine in the same minutes. Compare ratios, not times from different machines or days. `tests/reader_bench/baseline-6199085.tsv` is such a report for the revision in its name; its header names the machine. Set `MILO_BENCH_MAX_RATIO=1.25` to fail the run when a median is more than a quarter slower than the base's and the difference is more than noise: half a millisecond for a first frame, twenty microseconds for a key.

`tests/reader_bench.rs` and `tests/rex_lab.rs` use only what a built Milo offers from outside: its commands, what it draws in a terminal and, in the lab, the requests its browser editor accepts. So they can check a build they were not compiled with: set `MILO_TEST_BINARY` to a Milo built from another branch. Where a check depends on a feature that only some builds have, ask the build rather than the branch. The reader report's `syntax` column, for instance, says whether each build coloured each file as code, so a file in a language one build knows and the other does not is timed as code for the first and as plain text for the second.

## Commit messages

One line in the imperative that says what the commit does for someone using or reading milo ("Leave closed folders closed when work lands inside them"), then a short list of the notable changes if there are several. No ticket prefixes are needed.

## Reporting a bug

Use the **Bug report** form on GitHub; it adds the `bug` label. Say what you ran, what you saw and what you expected. If it depends on a repository's state, the smallest sequence of git commands that reproduces it is worth more than a description. A screenshot or pasted output helps but is optional; remove anything private first, such as tokens, account names, paths and repository contents, and give images alt text. For anything that looks like a security problem (milo running something, or showing something, that it should not), please report it privately to the maintainer rather than in a public issue.

To ask for something new, use the **Feature request** form, which adds `enhancement`. Describe the problem and the outcome you want; a design is not needed.

## Licence

By contributing you agree that your work is released under the MIT licence that covers the project (see `LICENSE`).

Source: https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/internals.md

# How milo works

Milo only reads a project, with one exception: the reader writes a file when you save an edit of it. It keeps the user's Git settings, such as global ignore rules, but overrides settings that could run a program. That includes hooks, content filters, external diff and text converters, file-system monitors and on-demand fetching. It caps Git's time and output. Git reports a change to the commit recorded for a submodule; milo does not inspect uncommitted or untracked files inside it.

The reader can show where a file link points without reading its target. It refuses a path through a folder link that leaves the project and does not read devices or pipes as files. Text from the project cannot send terminal controls.

## Writing

An edit is a draft in memory. A save opens the file from the project folder the reader holds, without following a link, checks that it is a regular file, and reads it again. It writes only if the file is the one the edit was read from and still holds the same bytes, or if the user answers the question that says it does not. The write goes into the open file, so its permissions, owner, other names and attributes are not touched, and each line keeps the ending it was read with. See [editing files](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#editing-files).

A formatter is a program of a fixed name, found in the folders of `PATH` that are written in full. It runs only when asked for, in a process group of its own, for at most ten seconds, with the draft on its standard input. It is not given the file to write. See [formatting](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/docs/panes.md#formatting).

Outside the project, milo keeps two things in its state folder for the editor: the draft of a reader that was ended with unsaved changes, and, in Rex, a mark that a floating reader has unsaved changes so that another pane does not replace it. The mark names the reader's process and is ignored once that process is gone.

## Updates and drawing

- One terminal loop handles replies, input, help and checks for changes. Pasted text is never read as keys: it is skipped, or handed whole to a pane that is taking text. If opening takes more than a moment, it draws `Reading…`; when it can identify a project, it shows its name too. A blocked loading-frame write yields once the pane is ready.
- On macOS, file-system notifications wake the Git panes. Outline and History filter writes to files and directories Git has reported as ignored. FSEvents excludes up to eight directories directly; Milo filters the remaining paths before waking a pane. The working reader uses its file's status and watches the wider project rather than reading all of Git status for exclusions. Watched panes check about every 30 seconds as a safety net; without notifications they check about every two seconds.
- A pane with nothing to watch, like setup or a reader at a commit, sleeps until input, a resize or a signal. Panes can also schedule a redraw without a file change. An ignored key does not rebuild the frame; terminal replies, resizes and scheduled checks do.
- After a check, milo waits at least four times as long as that check took, so repeated changes do not keep it busy indefinitely.
- The tracked file list is kept until the index changes, unpushed work is kept until the comparison changes, and commit file lists are cached once opened. Adding an unrelated untracked file does not require recounting edits in tracked files. With the same tracked status and comparison base, an ordinary save recounts only the edited files; changes that could affect rename detection or other files use the full comparison. A working reader reuses the Git status from its current refresh.
- Only changed screen cells are sent to the terminal, in one synchronised update. Milo asks for the background colour and uses it to shade the cursor and added or removed lines.
- Printable bases use Unicode 17.0.0 East Asian Width: wide and fullwidth characters take two cells; ambiguous characters take one. Combining marks stay with their base where applicable. Milo omits default-ignorable formatting characters, including emoji variation selectors, but preserves spacing Hangul fillers. Width is measured by scalar, not by full grapheme cluster.

The crate depends only on `libc`.

## Source map

The [source map](https://github.com/mcc0x/milo/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md#source-map) lists every source and test file.
